bullets: How a convergent boundary works: the denser plate sinks, pulls the rest behind it, and builds a trench, earthquakes and a volcanic arc
slides.heading: Subduction: slab-pull, trench and volcanic arc
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one oceanic plate as it sinks - and check who, if anyone, pushes it down.

bullets: Describe subduction at a convergent boundary: the denser oceanic plate bends down at the trench
Explain slab-pull as the force driving the plate, and correct the claim that the continental plate pushes it down
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to say what actually pulls the plate down.

bullets: The continental plate looks bigger and stronger, so it seems to shove the oceanic plate underneath it
But the oceanic plate sinks even where nothing touches it - so what is really doing the work?
slides.heading: Who pushes the plate down?
slides.notes: Ask the class: what pushes the oceanic plate down? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because scene 3 names the real force.

bullets: Oceanic plate rock is thinner but denser; continental plate rock is thicker but lighter
At a convergent boundary the denser plate is the one that sinks - this sinking is subduction
The deep fold where it dives is the ocean trench
slides.heading: Density decides who sinks
slides.notes: Stress the deciding property: density, not size. The lighter plate rides over; the denser plate goes under.

bullets: An oceanic plate and a continental plate move towards each other
The oceanic plate is denser, so it will be the one to sink
slides.heading: Two plates converge over the ocean
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the two plates meeting: note which one sits lower before anything bends.

bullets: Too dense to stay afloat, the leading edge of the oceanic plate bends downwards
The deep fold where it dives is the ocean trench
slides.heading: The denser plate bends down at the trench
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and trace the bend: the trench marks exactly where the plate turns down.

bullets: The sinking slab is heavy, so gravity pulls it down and it drags the rest of the plate behind it - slab-pull
As the slab cracks and grinds downwards, earthquakes fire along its path
slides.heading: Slab-pull drags the plate; earthquakes track the slab
slides.notes: Play scene 3 and follow the arrows: the slab pulls from below, and the earthquake markers trace its path down.

bullets: The slab heats up and releases water that melts the mantle above it
The magma rises and erupts, building a curved line of volcanoes parallel to the trench
slides.heading: Magma rises and builds a volcanic arc
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and connect the chain: sinking slab, melting above it, and an arc of volcanoes on the overriding plate.

bullets: If the continental plate pushed the oceanic plate down, the sinking should stop where the plates lose contact
But the slab keeps sinking and pulling far below the surface - so the push claim fails and slab-pull explains it
slides.heading: Worked example: testing the push claim at the trench
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, state the push claim. Step 2, the slab sinks hundreds of kilometres down, far beyond any push. Step 3, its own weight pulling - slab-pull - is the explanation that fits.

bullets: In pairs: put the trench, slab-pull, earthquakes and volcanic arc into one causal chain
Then swap and check: does the chain start with density and end with the arc?
slides.heading: Your turn: explain the chain
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for slab-pull named as the driver, then take two pairs answers.

bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who says the continental plate does the pushing
Name slab-pull as the real driver to earn full credit
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers say nothing pushes the plate down - it sinks and pulls.
